title: 01: Study on Road Accidents in Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area
text:
Public safety relies on coordinated action to protect communities and infrastructure from threats, including road traffic accidents. In rapidly growing urban centers like the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area, high vehicle density and complex road networks lead to marked spatial variations in traffic incidents. Because accidents are restricted to transportation channels, applying network-constrained spatial point-pattern analysis alongside standard geospatial analytics allows for evidence-based decision support for transportation safety and emergency management.
This is a study on road accidents in the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area, made up Bangkok, Nonthaburi, Nakhon Pathom, Pathum Thani, Samut Prakan and Samut Sakhon, for the purpose of applying geospatial analytics for public safety. The primary objectives are to:

Prepare, clean and integrate multi-source spatial, temporal and road network data within a defined study window.
Analyse first-order properties to model the spatial, temporal and network-constrained density distribution of traffic incidents.
Evaluate second-order network-constrained properties to distinguish significant accident blackspots on road segments from random occurrences.
Translate findings into actionable insights for public-safety planning and management.

text:
7. Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis: stpp methods
In this section, I will use functions from the stpp package to perform spatio-temporal point patterns analysis.

7.1 Preparing spatio-temporal point process object of stpp
Step 1: Extracting forest fire coordinates from the fire point events

coords <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)

Step 2: Creating a data frame by combining the x- and y-coordinates and temporal event. Note that the temporal event must be in integer.

fire_df <- data.frame(
  x = coords[, 1],  
  y = coords[, 2],
  t = fire_sf$`DayofYear`)

Step 3: Creating stpp spatio-temporal object
as.3dpoint() of stpp package is used to create stpp spatio-temporal object class. I will also confirm the object class and plot it.

fire_stpp <- as.3dpoints(fire_df)


class(fire_stpp)

[1] "stpp"



plot(fire_stpp)










7.2 Computing spatio-temporal k-function
STIKhat() of stpp package is used to compute space-time inhomogeneous K-function.

kbb_stik <- STIKhat(fire_stpp)

plotK() is used to visualise the output space-time inhomogeneous K-function.

plotK(kbb_stik)



7.3 Interpreting the Plot
If the contours show high values for small values of uu and vv, it suggests clustering at short spatial and temporal distances, meaning events occur close to each other in both space and time.
If the contours are flat or show low values, it indicates a more random distribution or a lack of significant clustering at those distances.
The spatial and temporal extent of clustering can be understood by observing how rapidly the contours increase or decrease as we move along the axes.






NoteNote



In interpreting the plot, I will first break down each part of the graph:

X-axis (u): Spatial distance (in spatial units, e.g., meters).
Y-axis (v): Temporal distance (in time units, e.g., days).
Contour Lines: The estimated value of the space-time K-function _{ST}(u, v). Higher values indicate a greater expected number of neighboring events occurring within spatial distance u and temporal distance v.

For small spatial and temporal intervals (u < 10,000 meters and v < 20 days), the contour values remain near zero, indicated by the absence of lines. The lack of high values at these small scales indicates an absence of strong localised space-time clustering at short distances and time frames. Instead, contour values increase progressively toward the upper-right quadrant, reaching values exceeding 3.5e12 at larger spatial distances (u > 30,000) and extended time (v > 60). This steady gradient demonstrates that event interaction is driven by patterns, such as seasonal weather conditions, rather than localised outbreaks. This is aligned with personal experiences, where haze conditions in Singapore due to regional forest fires tend to happen at certain times of the year.

3. Geospatial Data Wrangling
This section demonstrates how to transform sf point and polygon data frames using as.ppp() and as.owin(), preparing them for 1st- and 2nd-order spatial point pattern methods such as Kernel Density Estimation and nearest neighbor tests.






NoteNote



Before performing spatial point pattern analysis in R, standard simple feature (sf) objects must be converted into data structures recognised by the spatstat package. section: 4. Clark-Evan Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
text:
4. Clark-Evan Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
This section introduces the Clark-Evans test of aggregation to evaluate whether childcare services in Singapore follow a specific spatial pattern or are distributed purely by chance. As a key method in Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA), the Clark-Evans test measures the mean distance between each point feature and its nearest neighbour, summarising the pattern through the Clark-Evans aggregation index (R).
To test for spatial randomness, we evaluate the following two hypotheses at a 95% confidence level:

Ho = The distribution of childcare services are randomly distributed.
H1 = The distribution of childcare services are not randomly distributed.

By executing clarkevans.test() from the spatstat.explore package, we can formally quantify the spatial structure of these services to determine if they tend to group together in specific areas or spread out evenly across the country.

4.1 Perform the Clark-Evans test without CSR
The clarkevans.test() of spatstat.explore package can be performed with or without Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR). I will now do so without CSR.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"))


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








TipStatistical Conclusion



At a 95% confidence level, the Clark-Evans test gives a result of Clark-Evans aggregation index of R = 0.53532 and a p-value <2.2e-16. Because the p-value is well below the significance threshold of 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis.
The value of R indicates the underlying spatial structure of the point data:

R = 1: The spatial distribution is completely random.
R < 1: The spatial distribution exhibits clustering (points are closer to each other than expected by chance).
R = 0: Indicates complete clustering (all points at the exact same location).
R > 1: The spatial distribution exhibits dispersion or regularity (points are spread out uniformly).

Thus, with R < 1, we can conclude that the spatial distribution of childcare services across Singapore exhibits statistically significant spatial clustering rather than a random distribution.








TipBusiness Communication



The spatial analysis confirms that childcare centers in Singapore are heavily concentrated in specific geographic clusters rather than being evenly or randomly distributed across the country.

Targeted Expansion & Resource Allocation: Areas with low density or longer distances between facilities may indicate underserved communities. Educational authorities and urban planners can use these findings to identify service gaps and prioritise new childcare center in emerging residential areas.
Competitive Analysis for Operators: Private providers can leverage these spatial clustering patterns to identify market saturation in high-density areas and explore untapped regions where parents’ demand exceeds current capacity.

However, it should be noted that childcare centers may be absent or sparse in industrial or nature reserves, as there is little or no demand in these areas.




4.2 Perform the Clark-Evans test with CSR
I will now perform the test with CSR, using the argument method = “MonteCarlo”. Instead of assuming a standard distribution, this approach calculates the p-value by generating a specified number of simulated realisations from nsim, i.e., 99, of Complete Spatial Randomness based on the exact count of point events in our dataset. The observed Clark-Evans aggregation index R is then compared against the distribution of R values derived from these simulated CSR patterns to test our hypotheses.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








TipStatistical Conclusion



Both the section 4.1 test without CSR and the Monte Carlo simulation evaluate whether childcare services in Singapore follow a Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) pattern.
Both tests resulted in the same index of R = 0.53532. Because R < 1, it signals spatial clustering.
Without CSR, the p-value is <2.2e-16. With CSR, the p-value is 0.01. This is the lowest possible p-value for 99 simulations. At a 95% confidence level, both test approaches reject the null hypothesis of Complete Spatial Randomness. The test with CSR solidifies the test result, confirming that the spatial clustering of childcare centers across Singapore is statistically significant.








TipBusiness Communication



Similarly, spatial analysis confirms that childcare centers in Singapore are heavily concentrated in specific geographic clusters rather than being evenly or randomly distributed across the country. The test with CSR provides higher confidence for decision-makers by ensuring the observed spatial patterns hold true even under rigorous testing

title: 02a: First Order Spatial Points Analysis Methods
text:
5. Kernel Density Estimation Method
Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is an important tool in Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA), allowing us to transform discrete spatial points—such as the locations of childcare centers, into a smooth, continuous surface of spatial intensity. Unlike traditional statistical modeling that relies on strict distributional assumptions, KDE provides a non-parametric approach to visualise real-world spatial phenomena. By mapping variations in point density across Singapore, this technique enables us to transition from asking whether clustering exists to identifying exactly where these high-density hotspots and coverage deficits are, thus allowing for deeper spatial analysis.

5.1 Working with automatic bandwidth selection method
I will now compute a kernel density by using the following configurations of density() of spatstat:

bw.diggle() automatic bandwidth selection method. Other recommended methods are bw.CvL(), bw.scott() or bw.ppl().
The smoothing kernel used is gaussian, which is the default. Other smoothing methods are: “epanechnikov”, “quartic” or “disc”.
The intensity estimate is corrected for edge effect bias by using method described by Jones (1993) and Diggle (2010, equation 18.9). The default is FALSE.


kde_SG_diggle <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  sigma=bw.diggle,
  edge=TRUE,
  kernel="gaussian") 

I will now use the plot() function of Base R to display the kernel density derived.

plot(kde_SG_diggle)








The function summary() of Base R is used to print the summary report.

summary(kde_SG_diggle)

real-valued pixel image
128 x 128 pixel array (ny, nx)
enclosing rectangle: [2667.538, 55941.94] x [21448.47, 50256.33] units
dimensions of each pixel: 416 x 225.0614 units
Image is defined on a subset of the rectangular grid
Subset area = 669941961.12307 square units
Subset area fraction = 0.437
Pixel values (inside window):
    range = [-5.405685e-21, 3.063698e-05]
    integral = 1927.788
    mean = 2.877545e-06


I will also retrieve the bandwidth used to compute the kde layer.

bw <- bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp)
bw

   sigma 
295.9712 




5.2 Rescalling KDE values
I will now use rescale.ppp() ito covert the unit of measurement from meter to kilometer. This addresses the issue of SVY21 unit of measurement being in meter, which is too small to comprehend in the earlier plotted map in section 5.1.

childcareSG_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(
  childcareSG_ppp, 1000, "km")

I will now re-run density() using the re-scaled data set and plot the output kde map.

kde_childcareSG_km <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                              sigma=bw.diggle,
                              edge=TRUE,
                              kernel="gaussian")


plot(kde_childcareSG_km)








The map looks similar to the earlier one, but note the change in the legend.


5.3 Working with different automatic bandwidth methods
Besides bw.diggle(), there are three other spatstat functions that can be used to determine the bandwidth: bw.CvL(), bw.scott(), and bw.ppl().

bw.CvL(childcareSG_ppp_km)

   sigma 
4.357209 



bw.scott(childcareSG_ppp_km)

 sigma.x  sigma.y 
2.159749 1.396455 



bw.ppl(childcareSG_ppp_km)

   sigma 
0.378997 



bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp_km)

    sigma 
0.2959712 


Selecting an appropriate bandwidth is critical in KDE, as it directly determines the level of spatial smoothing applied to the point data. While automatic selection algorithms streamline this choice, different methods serve distinct analytical goals.

Likelihood Cross-Validation (bw.ppl()): As recommended by Baddeley et al. (2016), bw.ppl() is generally preferred for spatial patterns dominated by multiple tight clusters, as it prevents over-smoothing and preserves localised density variations.
Cross-Validation Criterion (bw.diggle()): In contrast, bw.diggle() is optimised for isolating a single, prominent cluster surrounded by random spatial noise.

I will now compare the two methods.

kde_childcareSG.ppl <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
                               sigma=bw.ppl, 
                               edge=TRUE,
                               kernel="gaussian")
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_km, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_childcareSG.ppl, main = "bw.ppl")










5.4 Working with different kernel methods
The default kernel method used in density.ppp() is gaussian. But there are three other options, namely: Epanechnikov, Quartic and Dics.
The code chunk below will be used to compute three more kernel density estimations by using these three kernel function.

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"), 
     main="Gaussian")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="epanechnikov"), 
     main="Epanechnikov")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="quartic"), 
     main="Quartic")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="disc"), 
     main="Disc")

6. Fixed and Adaptive KDE

6.1 Computing KDE by using fixed bandwidth
I will compute a KDE layer by defining a bandwidth of 600 meter. The sigma value used is 0.6 as the unit of measurement of childcareSG_ppp_km object is in kilometer. This means that the 600m is 0.6km.

kde_childcareSG_fb <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                              sigma=0.6, 
                              edge=TRUE,
                              kernel="gaussian")
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb)










6.2 Computing KDE by using adaptive bandwidth
The fixed bandwidth method is very sensitive to highly skewed distribution of spatial point patterns over geographical units, e.g., urban versus rural. One way to overcome this is to use adaptive bandwidth.
I will derive the adaptive kernel density estimation by using density.adaptive() of spatstat.

kde_childcareSG_ab <- adaptive.density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km, 
  method="kernel")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab)








I will compare the fixed and adaptive kernel density estimation outputs.

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")

4. Plotting the Geospatial Data
Using plot(), you can visualise a data frame by generating coloured maps based on different attributes

plot(mpsz)








The default plot of an sf object is a multi-plot of all attributes, up to a reasonable maximum as shown above. This includes visualisation of non-informative features, such as OBJECTID_1.
Instead, you can plot only the geometry by using st_geometry() where only the shape and not the attributes are mapped out.

plot(st_geometry(mpsz))








We can also plot using a specific attribute, such as PLN_AREA_N.

plot(mpsz["PLN_AREA_N"])








When you have more than one layer, you can plot them ontop of each other to visualise more information. I will now plot preschool layer ontop of the mpsz layer.

plot(st_geometry(mpsz))
plot(st_geometry(preschool), 
     add = TRUE)














NoteNote



As both preschool and mpsz are in WGS84, the preschool points appear on the subzone map. However, the points are too dense and it is difficult to have a detailed interpretation of the exact locations within each subzone. Regardless, it provides a good overview of where preschools are generally not located, namely the industrial areas, nature reserves and offshore islands.


Let’s now try plotting the cyclingpath layer ontop of the mpsz layer, where the former is in SVY21 while the latter is in WGS84.

plot(st_geometry(mpsz))
plot(st_geometry(cyclingpath),
     add = TRUE, col = "Blue")








Cycling path lines do not appear on the subzone layer due to the different coordinate system used. Hence, projection transformation will need to be performed in order to geoprocess these two sets of data.

5. Working with Projection

5.1 Transforming projection of mpsz and preschool from WGS84 to SVY21
When analysis of geospatial data involves the use of distance and/or area measurement, we will need to transform data from geographic coordinate system to projected coordinate system. The transformation uses the st_transform() package, where the reprojection to another coordinate system is done mathematically.






NoteNote



SVY21 is Singapore’s official national horizontal geodetic datum and plane coordinate system, and is based on the WGS84 (World Geodetic System 1984) to flatten the curved surface of Earth into metric measurements. We will be referencing an EPSG code to identify specific coordinate reference system (CRS), which in the case of SVY21 is 3414.



mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 
                              crs = 3414)

st_geometry(mpsz)

cyclingpath <- st_transform(cyclingpath, crs = 3414)

Projection transformation to SVY21 have been completed for mpsz and preschool, and they are now ready to be geoprocessed with cyclingpath and included for analysis involving distance and area measurements.

7. Geoprocessing with sf package
Besides functions to handle geospatial data, such as importing, assigning projections and transformations which were shown earlier, sf package offers a wide range of geoprocessing functions. This is also known as Geographic Information System (GIS) analysis.

7.1 Use Case 1: land acquisition analysis
Scenario The authority is planning to upgrade the exiting cycling path. To do so, they need to acquire 5 meters of reserved land on both sides of the existing cycling path. You are tasked to determine the extend of the land that needs to be acquired and the total area.
Solution First, I will use st_buffer to compute the 5-meter buffer around the cycling paths. The function is used to expand or shrink vector geometries outward by a specified distance, where the width is defined by the dist= referencing the metrics of SVY21. nQuadSegs controls the smoothness of and must be an integer more than or equals to 1. Although there is no upper limit, high values may produce negligible visual improvement.

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(
  cyclingpath, dist=5, nQuadSegs = 30)

I will now calculate the area of the buffer using tidyverse.

buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))

Lastly, I will use sum() to derive the total land needed

sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

3687875 [m^2]


The buffer can also be plotted based on a selected planning subzone for the purpose of land acqusition planning, such as Tampines West .
First, I will use filter() to extract the polygon feature of Tampines West.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

Next, I will use st_intersection() to clip the cycling buffers within Tampines West planning subzone.

buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(
  buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)

Lastly, I will use plot() to create the plot as shown below.

plot(st_geometry(buffer_cycling_selected))










7.2 Use case 2: To determine the number of pre-schools by planning subzone
Scenario The authority requires a count of pre-schools for each planning subzone to support forward planning. Using R and the sf package, perform the necessary geoprocessing to compute these counts and present the results clearly.
Solution First, to identify pre-schools located inside each Planning Subzone by using st_intersects(). Next, length() is used to calculate numbers of pre-schools that fall inside each planning subzone.

mpsz$`PreSch Count`<- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool))

title: 01b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Thematic mapping involves the use of map symbols to visualise properties of geographic features that are not naturally visible, such as population, temperature, crime rate and property prices.
Geovisualisation, on the other hand, is the process of using visual representations and cartographic techniques to explore, analyse and communicate geospatial data. It combines elements of cartography, computer science and information visualisation to enhance spatial understanding and knowledge discovery.
In this chapter, I will plot functional and truthful choropleth maps by using an R package called tmap package.

title: 01b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
1. Importing Packages and Data

1.1 Importing packages
Aside from the tmap package, I will also be importing sf, tidyverse and rvest.

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse, rvest)



1.2 Importing data into R
I will be using the below two data sets to create the choropleth map:

Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea). This shows the geographical boundary of Singapore at the planning subzone level and is based on URA Master Plan 2019. The format is in GEOJSON and I will be converting it to KML format.
Singapore residents by planning area / subzone, age group, sex and type of dwelling, June 2024 in csv format. This is an aspatial data file downloaded from Department of Statistics, Singapore. Although it does not contain any coordinates values, its PA and SZ fields can be used as unique identifiers to georeference to the planning subzone data set.



1.3 Importing geospatial data into R
Using the st_read() of sf package, I will be importing the polygon feature layer in GeoJSON format file MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL into R. will also be converting it from a GeoJSON format to KML format using the st_write() function.

         driver = "KML", delete_dsn = FALSE) #write files in KML format and prevent overwrite

Tidying is required for KML files because their attribute data is embedded as an HTML table within a single description field, rather than being split into individual columns. The extraction step is needed to parse out values like REGION_N and SUBZONE_N into proper, usable columns.






NoteNote

1.4 Importing attribute data into R
I will now import the respopagesextod2024.csv file into RStudio and save the file into a tibble dataframe called popdata.
The task will be performed by using read_csv() function of readr package.

popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv")



1.5 Data preparation
Before preparing a thematic map, I will prepare a data table with values from year 2020. The data table should include the variables PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL and DEPENDENCY.

YOUNG: age group 0 to 4 until age groyup 20 to 24,
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age group 25-29 until age group 60-64,
AGED: age group 65 and above,
TOTAL: all age group, and
DEPENDENCY: the ratio between young and aged against economy active group

I will be using the following data wrangling and transformation functions:

pivot_wider() of tidyr package, and
mutate(), filter(), group_by() and select() of dplyr package


popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup()%>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
/`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
       `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
       `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)

Before joining the datasets, I will convert the PA and SZ fields to uppercase. Their values currently mix upper- and lowercase, whereas SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N use uppercase letters.

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ), 
          .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

Next, I will perform the join using left_join() from dplyr, using the subzone names SUBZONE_N and SZ as the common identifier to combine the geographical and attribute data.

mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

It should be noted that passing the mpsz simple feature data frame as the left table in left_join() ensures that the resulting output retains its spatial properties and remains a simple feature object.
I will now save the R object mpsz_pop2024 as a .rds file, so that I can reload it later without having to redo all the earlier processing steps.

write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/geospatial/mpsz_pop2024.rds")

title: 01b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
section: 2. Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap
text:
2. Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap
Choropleth mapping uses area patterns or graduated colors to visualise data across geographic units like countries, states or subzones.
In tmap, I can create thematic maps using two approaches:

Quick maps with qtm(): Fast and simple for default visualisations.
Custom maps with tmap elements: Offers full control over design and layering.


2.1 Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using qtm()
qtm() is the easiest way to quickly draw a choropleth map. It usually provides a good default visualisation. I will be producing a static map using the plot option, whereas an interactive one can be produced using the view option. I will also be using DEPENDENCY as the attribute in fill=.

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")










2.2 Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
While qtm() is great for creating choropleth maps quickly, it makes fine-tuning layer aesthetics difficult. For higher-quality, cartographic-standard maps, build your visualisation using tmap’s individual drawing elements instead.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by Planning Subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and population data from Department of Statistics (DOS)", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










2.3 Drawing a base map
The core building block of tmap starts with tm_shape() to define your input dataset, followed by one or more layer elements such as tm_polygons(), tm_symbols(), tm_lines(), tm_raster() or tm_text().
I will be using tm_shape() to define the input data and tm_polygons() to draw the planning subzone polygons. By default, the areas of polygons is in light gray (gray85) and polygons borders are in slightly dark gray (gray25).

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()










2.4 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_polygons()
I will be drawing a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone. The variable DEPENDENCY will be assigned to tm_polygons().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")










2.5 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_fill() and tm_border()
tm_polygons() is infact a wraper of tm_fill() and tm_border(). tm_fill() is to fill the polygons using the default colour scheme and tm_borders() adds the borders of the polygon features. Here is what the map would look like without and with tm_borders().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()








We can also change the border colour, border line width and border line type accordingly.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")










2.6 Data classification methods of tmap
Choropleth maps group large datasets into distinct classes or ranges using data classification techniques.
The tmap package offers ten classification methods: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (the default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher and jenks.
The style arguments tm_fill() or tm_polygons() can be used to define a data classification method.

2.6.1 Plotting choropleth maps with built-in classification methods
I will be using the style argument of tm_fill() or tm_polygons() to define a data classification method. Here is how a quantile data classification using 5 classes is done.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Here is where I use an equal data classification method.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)














NoteNote



For this instance, we will notice that the distribution using the quantile data classification method is more evenly distributed:

Quantile Classification: Divides the total number of geographic features (polygons) into equal-sized groups. If you request 5 classes, it places roughly 20% of the subzones into each group. Because it assigns a fixed count of features to every class, the resulting colors are distributed evenly across the map regardless of skew in the underlying numbers.
Equal Interval Classification: Divides the range of data values (from minimum to maximum value) into equal-sized numerical intervals. It ignores how many polygons fall into each interval. If your data contains extreme outliers or is heavily skewed toward low values, most subzones end up clumped into just one or two color categories, leaving the remaining classes nearly empty.





2.6.2 DIY 1: Comparing Data Classification Methods
Here, I will compare four different data classification methods (quantile, equal, jenks and sd) using a fixed 5-class scale to see how class boundary calculations change the spatial distribution of the DEPENDENCY ratio.

map_quantile <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Quantile")

map_equal <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Equal")

map_jenks <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Jenks")

map_sd <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "sd", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Standard Deviation")

# arrange in a 2x2 grid layout
tmap_arrange(map_quantile, map_equal, map_jenks, map_sd, ncol = 2)














NoteNote



The following were observed from the four maps:

Quantile: Spreads subzones evenly across the color bins, so the map shows a nice mix of colors. The downside is it can hide extreme cases or make small, unimportant differences look bigger than they are.
Equal Interval: Splits the value range into equal-sized chunks. Since a few subzones have unusually high dependency ratios, most other subzones get squeezed into the lowest bin. This results in the map ending up mostly with one color, with barely anything in the higher bins.
Jenks (Natural Breaks): Groups similar values together and keeps different groups apart, so it naturally finds where the real breaks in the data are. This makes it good at showing genuine clusters, especially when the data is not evenly spread out.
Standard Deviation: Shows which subzones sit unusually far above or below the average dependency ratio. This is useful for quickly spotting the outliers.





2.6.3 DIY 2: Comparing Different Number of Classes
Using a single classification method (quantile), I will vary the number of classes (n = 2, 6, 10, 20) to observe how it affects map readability and data interpretation.

map_c2 <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 2)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("2 Classes")

map_c6 <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 6)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("6 Classes")

map_c10 <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("10 Classes")

map_c20 <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 20)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("20 Classes")

# Arrange in a 2x2 grid layout
tmap_arrange(map_c2, map_c6, map_c10, map_c20, ncol = 2)














NoteNote



The following were observed from the four maps:

2 Classes: Splits everything into just “high” or “low,” which is easy to read at a glance but loses the details.
6 Classes: Seems to strike a balance between visual clarity and details.
10–20 Classes: The shades are become too subtle in differences, making it difficult to visually differentiate.





2.6.4 Plotting choropleth map with custom break
By default, tmap calculates category breaks automatically. To set custom intervals instead, we will need to indicate values to the breaks argument in tm_scale_intervals(). Before choosing custom breakpoints, it is best practice to inspect the data’s summary statistics.

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
 0.2500  0.7523  0.8407  0.8776  0.9368 12.7500      90 


Based on the result, I will set break points at at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90, and include a minimum and maximum of 0 and 100. The breaks vector will be c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00).

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











2.7 Colour scheme
tmap also supports colour ramps as defined by users or based on a set of predefined colour ramps from the RColorBrewer package.

2.7.1 Using ColorBrewer palette

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








We will need to add a “-” prefix to reverse the shading of the map based on the DEPENDENCY attribute.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










2.7.2 Cartographic Furniture
tmap also can be used to draw other map furnitures, such as compass, scale bar, grid lines and data sources using tm_compass(), tm_scale_bar(), tm_grid() and tm_credit().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))











2.8 Map Layout
Map layout is the coming together of map elements to form a cohesive map. This can be customised using the tm_layout() function.

2.8.1 Map Legend

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_pos_auto_in() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










2.8.2 Map Style

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tmap_style("natural")

title: 01b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
3. Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Maps can also be stacked vertically, arranged side-by-side or in grids, as demonstrated in 2.6.2 and 2.6.3. This allows the visualisation of relationships change based on a variable, such as time.

3.1 By assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments
By assigning two variables to the visual variable.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) + 
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
    fill.legend = 
      tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in(
        "right", "bottom")),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal", 
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")










3.2 By arranging multiples choropleth maps in a grid layout

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                  item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")
                
agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              style = "quantile", 
              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp=1, ncol=2)










3.3 By defining a group-by variable in tm_facets()

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) + 
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2, 
            ncols = 3,
            free.coords=TRUE, 
            drop.units=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

4. Mappping Spatial Object Meeting a Selection Criterion
filter() can be used to select a certain geographical area and to plot a choropleth map on the selected region. I will plot this based on CENTRAL REGION.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend()) +

section: 5. Complementing Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
text:
5. Complementing Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
Maps and statistical charts can complement each other to represent different aspects of the same data, thus enhancing a reader’s understanding.
tmap can be used to include statistical chart into the map visualisation by using the fill.chart argument to include box plot.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)








I will be improving the visual representation by highlighting and labelling the outliers on the choropleth map.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY)

outlier_vals <- stats$out

outlier_sf <- mpsz_selected[mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tm_shape(mpsz_selected) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile", 
            values = "brewer.blues"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(),
          fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "darkred", lwd = 3) +
  tm_text("SUBZONE_N", col = "red", size = 1) +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)

title: 01b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
6. Creating Interactive Map
Interactive maps are useful in letting users explore the data based on their requirements and to gain a better understanding of the information. tmap_mode() allows you to switch easily between static and interactive maps.
I will modify the code from section 4 to build an interactive map.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2)






Without limiting the set_zoom_limits argument, users might have difficulty navigating the map.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")

tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12,14))

title: 01b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R

I will first install the relevant R packages.

  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414) %>%

write_rds(mpsz_cl, "data/mpsz_cl.rds")

I will now import the Childcare Service GeoJSON file as an sf data frame called childcare_sf and transform the EPSG to 3414.

spatstat requires the point event data in ppp object form. I will now be converting childcare_sf to a ppp format childcare_ppp.

childcare_ppp <- as.ppp(childcare_sf)

I will extract the target planning areas, i.e., Punggol, Tampines Chua Chu Kang and Jurong West.

pg <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "PUNGGOL")

  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "TAMPINES")

  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "CHOA CHU KANG")

  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "JURONG WEST")

pg_owin = as.owin(pg)
tm_owin = as.owin(tm)
ck_owin = as.owin(ck)
jw_owin = as.owin(jw)

childcare_ck_ppp = childcare_ppp[ck_owin]

childcare_pg_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_pg_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_tm_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_tm_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_ck_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_ck_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_jw_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_jw_ppp, 1000, "km")

I will now plot these four areas and the locations of the childcare centres.

  main="Punggol")
plot(unmark(childcare_tm_ppp.km), 
  main="Tampines")
plot(unmark(childcare_ck_ppp.km), 
  main="Choa Chu Kang")
plot(unmark(childcare_jw_ppp.km), 
  main="Jurong West")

2. Second-Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis

2.1 Analysing Spatial Point Process Using G Function
The G function measures the distribution of the distances from an arbitrary event to its nearest event. In this section, I will compute G-function estimation by using Gest() of spatstat package. I will also be performing the Monte Carlo simulation test using envelope() of spatstat package.






NoteNote



The G function is cumulative and increases as the distance increases. We can obtain information on point pattern clusters based on the shape of the G function, i.e., G function increases rapidly at short distances for clustered points, and increases slowly up to the distance which most points are spaced before increasing rapidly if points are dispersed.
Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) is a computational technique that uses random sampling and probability distributions to model complex systems under uncertainty (Oshan, 2025).
In urban planning, MCS serves as a critical tool for modeling spatial point patterns, land-use dynamics, and service demand under shifting socio-demographic conditions (Oshan, 2025). When applied to the distribution of childcare centres in Singapore, MCS allows planners to test for CSR and run simulation models in a location. Through this, we can determine whether clusters or gaps are significant events or random, leading to more robust facility planning.



2.1.1 Choa Chu Kang planning area

set.seed(1234)


G_CK = Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border")
plot(G_CK, xlim=c(0,500))














NoteNote



The black line rises rapidly at a short distance and is mostly above the red line (Poisson process), thus suggesting a clustered pattern.


To confirm the observed spatial patterns above, I will conduct a hypothesis test using the Monte Carlo simulation. The hypothesis and test are as follows:
Ho = The distribution of childcare services at Choa Chu Kang are randomly distributed.
H1= The distribution of childcare services at Choa Chu Kang are not randomly distributed.
The null hypothesis will be rejected if p-value is smaller than the alpha value of 0.001.

4 Computing distance based neighbours
I will now derive distance-based weight matrices by using dnearneigh() of spdep package.
The function identifies neighbours of region points by Euclidean distance with a distance band with lower d1= and upper d2= bounds controlled by the bounds= argument. If unprojected coordinates are used, and either specified in the coordinates object x or with x as a two column matrix and longlat=TRUE, great circle distances in km will be calculated assuming the WGS84 reference ellipsoid.

4.1 Determine the cut-off distance
First, I will need to determine the upper limit for distance band:

Return a matrix with the indices of points belonging to the set of the k nearest neighbours of each other by using knearneigh() of spdep.
Convert the knn object returned by knearneigh() into a neighbours list of class nb with a list of integer vectors containing neighbour region number ids by using knn2nb().
Return the length of neighbour relationship edges by using nbdists() of spdep. The function returns in the units of the coordinates if the coordinates are projected, in km otherwise.
Remove the list structure of the returned object by using unlist().


#coords <- coordinates(hunan)
k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  24.79   32.57   38.01   39.07   44.52   61.79 


The summary report shows that the largest first nearest neighbour distance is 61.79 km. Using this as the upper threshold gives certainty that all units will have at least one neighbour.

6. Row-standardised Weights Matrix
Next, I will assign weights to each neighboring polygon. In our case, each neighboring polygon will be assigned equal weight using style=“W”. This is accomplished by assigning the fraction 1/(#ofneighbors) to each neighboring county then summing the weighted income values. While this is the most intuitive way to summarise the neighbors’ values, the drawback is that polygons along the edges of the study area will base their lagged values on fewer polygons thus potentially over- or under-estimating the true nature of the spatial autocorrelation in the data. For this example, we will stick with the style=“W” option for simplicity’s sake but note that other more robust options are available, notably style=“B”.

text:
4. Network KDE (NKDE) Analysis
I will perform NKDE analysis by using appropriate functions provided in spNetwork package.

4.1 Preparing the lixels objects
Before computing NKDE, the SpatialLines object need to be cut into lixels with a specified minimal distance. This task can be performed using lixelize_lines() of spNetwork:

The length of a lixel, lx_length is set to 700m.
The minimum length of a lixel, mindist is set to 350m.

After cut, if the length of the final lixel is shorter than the minimum distance, it is added to the previous lixel. If NULL, then mindist = maxdist/10. Also note that the segments that are already shorter than the minimum distance are not modified.

lixels <- lixelize_lines(network, 
                         700, 
                         mindist = 375)



4.2 Generating line centre points
Next, lines_center() of spNetwork will be used to generate a SpatialPointsDataFrame (i.e. samples) with line centre points. The points are located at center of the line based on the length of the line.

samples <- lines_center(lixels) 



4.3 Performing NKDE
I will now compute the NKDE:

kernel_name argument indicates that quartic kernel is used. Possible kernel methods supported by spNetwork are triangle, gaussian, scaled gaussian, tricube, cosine ,triweight, epanechnikov and uniform.
method argument indicates that simple method is used to calculate the NKDE. Currently, spNetwork support three popular methods, they are:

method=“simple”. This first method was presented by Xie et al. (2008) and proposes an intuitive solution. The distances between events and sampling points are replaced by network distances, and the formula of the kernel is adapted to calculate the density over a linear unit instead of an areal unit.
method=“discontinuous”. The method is proposed by Okabe et al (2008), which equally “divides” the mass density of an event at intersections of lixels.
method=“continuous”. If the discontinuous method is unbiased, it leads to a discontinuous kernel function which is a bit counter-intuitive. Okabe et al (2008) proposed another version of the kernel, that divide the mass of the density at intersection but adjusts the density before the intersection to make the function continuous.



densities <- nkde(network, 
                  events = childcare,
                  w = rep(1, nrow(childcare)),
                  samples = samples,
                  kernel_name = "quartic",
                  bw = 300, 
                  div= "bw", 
                  method = "simple", 
                  digits = 1, 
                  tol = 1,
                  grid_shape = c(1,1), 
                  max_depth = 8,
                  agg = 5, 
                  sparse = TRUE,
                  verbose = FALSE)


4.3.1 Visualising NKDE
Before I can visualise the NKDE values, I will insert the computed density values (i.e. densities) into samples and lixels objects as density fields.

samples$density <- densities
lixels$density <- densities

Since svy21 projection system is in meters, the computed density values are very small i.e. 0.0000005. I will rescale the density values from number of events per meter to number of events per kilometer.

samples$density <- samples$density*1000
lixels$density <- lixels$density*1000

I will use appropriate functions of tmap package to prepare interactive and high cartographic quality map visualisation.

tmap_mode('view')
tm_shape(lixels)+
  tm_lines(col="density")+
tm_shape(childcare)+
  tm_dots()






The interactive map above reveals road segments (darker colour) with relatively higher density of childcare centres than road segments with relatively lower density of childcare centres (lighter colour).

section: 5. Network Constrained G- and K-Function Analysis
text:
5. Network Constrained G- and K-Function Analysis
In this section, I will perform complete spatial randomness (CSR) test by using kfunctions() of spNetwork package. The null hypothesis is defined as:

Ho: The observed spatial point events (i.e distribution of childcare centres) are uniformly distributed over a street network in Punggol Planning Area.

The CSR test is based on the assumption of the binomial point process which implies the hypothesis that childcare centres are randomly and independently distributed over the street network.
If this hypothesis is rejected, we may infer that the distribution of childcare centres are spatially interacting and dependent on each other. As a result, they may form non-random patterns.
There are nine arguments used:

lines: A SpatialLinesDataFrame with the sampling points. The geometries must be a SpatialLinesDataFrame (may crash if some geometries are invalid).
points: A SpatialPointsDataFrame representing the points on the network. These points will be snapped on the network.
start: A double, the start value for evaluating the k and g functions.
end: A double, the last value for evaluating the k and g functions.
step: A double, the jump between two evaluations of the k and g function.
width: The width of each donut for the g-function.
nsim: An integer indicating the number of Monte Carlo simulations required. In the above example, 50 simulation was performed. Note: most of the time, more simulations are required for inference
resolution: When simulating random points on the network, selecting a resolution will reduce greatly the calculation time. When resolution is null the random points can occur everywhere on the graph. If a value is specified, the edges are split according to this value and the random points are selected vertices on the new network.
conf_int: A double indicating the width confidence interval (default = 0.05).


kfun_childcare <- kfunctions(network, 
                             childcare,
                             start = 0, 
                             end = 1000, 
                             step = 50, 
                             width = 50, 
                             nsim = 50, 
                             resolution = 50,
                             verbose = FALSE, 
                             conf_int = 0.05)

The output of kfunctions() is a list with the following values:

plotkA, a ggplot2 object representing the values of the k-function
plotgA, a ggplot2 object representing the values of the g-function
valuesA, a DataFrame with the values used to build the plots

For example, we can visualise the ggplot2 object of k-function.

kfun_childcare$plotk








The blue line is the empirical network K-function of the childcare centres in Punggol planning area. The gray envelop represents the results of the 50 simulations in the interval 2.5% - 97.5%. Because the blue line between the distance of 0 to 250 metres are above the gray area, we can infer that there is statistically significant spatial clustering at short distances (up to ~250 meters). There are more childcare centres located within 250 meters of one another along the network than would be expected by pure chance.
